articles.summary: August is when your hair can start noticing fall before you do. Summer asks your hair to navigate heat, humidity, UV exposure, sweat, and frequent styling. As the season changes, cooler temperatures and lower humidity change the environment around the hair fiber, too. By September and October, a routine designed primarily to manage summer humidity may no longer be addressing what your hair needs most. But that doesn't mean you need an entirely new routine. It means understanding how your hair structure responds to its environment and adjusting where your routine puts its focus. Because hair isn't random. Its behavior is largely determined by its structure, and that structure responds to moisture, friction, heat, humidity, and the condition of the cuticle. Why the Summer-to-Fall Transition Matters for Your Hair The outer layer of your hair, the cuticle, acts as a protective barrier. Along with the hair's natural lipid layer, it helps regulate how moisture moves into and out of the fiber. When that surface system is intact, hair is better able to resist excess water. When it becomes compromised by heat, chemical processing, friction, or environmental stress, moisture movement becomes less controlled. That's when you may notice roughness, dryness, frizz, or a loss of definition. Humidity adds another layer to the equation. Inside the cortex, hydrogen bonds are temporary connections that help maintain the shape of the hair. Water can break and reform these bonds, which is why humidity can change how hair behaves. When moisture enters the fiber unevenly, the hair can swell and shift shape, creating the frizz and flyaways associated with humid weather. As the air becomes drier, the problem can change. Instead of primarily managing excess moisture coming from the environment, your routine increasingly needs to help retain moisture within the hair. Dry air also makes static more noticeable because electrical charges don't dissipate as easily. Friction from sweaters, hats, scarves, pillowcases, and brushing can make those flyaways even more obvious. That doesn't mean every hair type needs the same amount of moisture. In fact, this is where hair type matters most. Straight Hair: Keep Cleansing Balanced, Add Lightweight Protection Straight hair has a relatively uniform fiber structure, so sebum can travel easily from the scalp toward the ends. That's one reason straight hair can become oily or look weighed down faster than other hair types. At the same time, over-washing can contribute to dryness, particularly through the lengths and ends. As fall approaches, the goal isn't to suddenly stop cleansing. It's to balance cleansing with moisture retention. Continue focusing shampoo on the scalp, where oil and buildup accumulate, while keeping heavier conditioning products away from the roots. Depending on scalp activity, straight hair may need cleansing every one to three days. Then add lightweight protection to the lengths. A leave-in treatment on damp hair can provide light moisture and help reduce flyaways without overwhelming the strand. For a finishing step, a lightweight serum can smooth the surface, add shine, and provide a protective layer against dryness and static. Your fall focus: hydration without weight, balanced cleansing, and protection for dry ends. Try: Custom Straight Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Straight Hair Mask once a week, Straight Hair Leave-In, and Custom Hair Serum. Wavy Hair: Move From Humidity Control to Moisture Balance Wavy hair sits in the middle of the spectrum. Its S-shaped pattern creates bends along the fiber, which means sebum doesn't travel as evenly as it does along straight hair. The result can be familiar: oily roots, dry ends, and a wave pattern that seems to have a mind of its own. In summer, humidity can disrupt those waves by changing the temporary bonds inside the cortex. In fall, lower humidity can shift the problem toward dryness, static, and loss of definition. The answer isn't simply adding the heaviest product you can find. Wavy hair benefits from balanced moisture that supports the wave without stretching it out. Keep cleansing gentle and focus shampoo on the scalp. On days when your hair doesn't need a full wash, refreshing with conditioner or a lightweight leave-in can help maintain moisture without repeatedly cleansing the strand. As the air gets drier, your mask can also become more important. The Wavy Hair Mask with vegan squalane provides deeper conditioning for waves that are feeling dry or more prone to frizz. For styling, apply your wave-defining product to soaking-wet or damp hair and scrunch rather than brushing through afterward. That helps preserve the natural wave pattern instead of breaking it apart. Your fall focus: balanced moisture, wave definition, and less friction. Try: Custom Wavy Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Wavy Hair Leave-In Treatment, Wavy Hair Mask one to two times a week as needed, and Zero-Gravity Styling Mousse for definition. Curly Hair: Prioritize Moisture Retention, Not Just Hydration Curly hair has a structural challenge that doesn't disappear when summer ends: the bends and curves in the fiber make it harder for natural oils to travel from the scalp to the ends. That's why curly hair can feel dry even when the scalp doesn't. The shape of the fiber also means the cuticle is less uniformly aligned, which can make moisture move in and out more readily. Dryness isn't a sign that your hair is doing something wrong. It's geometry. Fall makes moisture retention even more important. Rather than simply adding more water-based hydration, think about what happens after hydration. A leave-in treatment helps maintain moisture throughout the day, while a curl cream conditions the surface of the strand and helps support definition. Layering products allows you to build the amount of moisture and control your individual curls need. As fall progresses, make deep conditioning a consistent part of your routine. The Curly Hair Mask, formulated with coconut oil and shea butter, provides more intensive conditioning for curls that are feeling dry or less defined. And keep friction low. Avoid dry brushing, detangle while conditioning, and consider a silk or satin pillowcase to reduce friction and moisture loss while you sleep. Your fall focus: moisture retention, definition, low friction, and consistent conditioning. Try: Custom Curly Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Curly Hair Mask, Curly Leave-In Treatment, and Super Shape Curl Cream. Coily Hair: Protect the Moisture You've Worked to Keep Coily hair has the most complex pathway for natural oils to travel. Tight bends and turns create more points of friction and stress along the strand, while the cuticle is more separated and less uniformly aligned. That makes coily hair particularly susceptible to moisture loss, dryness, and breakage. Again, this isn't a flaw. It's the physics of the fiber. When humidity drops, moisture retention becomes even more important. For coily hair, the goal should be less about repeatedly adding moisture and more about keeping that moisture in the fiber. Gentle cleansing helps preserve the hair's surface lipids, while rich conditioning and leave-in products provide ongoing support. Coily hair generally benefits from less frequent cleansing—often every five to seven days depending on scalp needs and lifestyle—with shampoo concentrated primarily on the scalp. After conditioning, layer your leave-in while the hair is still wet, followed by your styling product. For additional protection, a serum can provide another surface layer that helps reduce moisture loss, friction, and static. As fall moves toward winter, protective styling and low-manipulation routines become increasingly useful for minimizing mechanical stress. Your fall focus: moisture retention, lipid support, low manipulation, and protection from friction. Try: Coily Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Coily Hair Mask, Coily Leave-In Treatment, and Custom Hair Serum. One Important Note About Porosity You may have heard that straight hair is low porosity and curly or coily hair is high porosity. There's some structural reasoning behind those tendencies, but hair type and porosity aren't the same thing. Porosity describes how easily hair absorbs and retains moisture, and it's influenced by the condition of the cuticle. Damage from chemical processing, heat, friction, and environmental stress can change how porous hair behaves. Two people with the same curl pattern can therefore have very different moisture needs. That's why your routine should respond to both your hair type and your hair's current condition. If your waves suddenly feel dry, your curls aren't holding, or your straight hair feels rough at the ends, don't assume you need an entirely different routine. Look at what your hair is telling you about moisture retention, surface condition, buildup, and friction. The Fall Hair Rule: Follow the Structure The biggest seasonal shift isn't about replacing your entire summer routine. It's about changing what your routine is designed to do. In summer, your hair may need more support against humidity, heat, UV exposure, and environmental moisture. In fall, lower humidity and increasing friction can make moisture retention, conditioning, and static management more important. And the right adjustment depends on your hair's structure. Straight: Keep it light. Balance cleansing with hydration and protect the ends. Wavy: Keep the balance. Add conditioning without sacrificing your wave pattern. Curly: Layer moisture and focus on retaining it. Coily: Prioritize moisture sealing, low manipulation, and protection. Your hair doesn't need to follow the calendar perfectly. It just needs a routine that understands how its structure responds when the environment changes. Because great hair care isn't about fighting your hair. It's about understanding it.
articles.title: How to Transition Your Hair Routine From Summer to Fall, by Hair Type

articles.summary: Silicone has become one of the most misunderstood ingredients in hair care. Today, "silicone-free" appears on countless product labels, often alongside claims like "sulfate-free" and "paraben-free." But unlike a trend, hair biology doesn't change. For years, silicones have been praised for delivering slip and shine… and criticized for causing buildup and dullness. So which is it? The truth is, silicone isn't inherently good or bad for your hair. Its performance depends on the type of silicone, the formula it's used in, and most importantly, your hair type. At Function of Beauty, we believe understanding how ingredients work is more valuable than avoiding them based on a label. Here's what silicone actually does and when it can be beneficial. What Does Silicone Do for Hair? Every strand of hair is protected by a layer called the cuticle. Think of it as your hair's outer shield. It controls how moisture moves in and out of the strand, influences shine, and plays a major role in how smooth—or frizzy—your hair feels. Silicones form a lightweight film over the cuticle that helps support its natural function. Depending on the formula, they can: Smooth the cuticle to reduce friction between strands Minimize frizz and static Increase shine by creating a smoother surface that reflects light Help protect hair from heat styling Slow excess moisture movement that contributes to frizz in humid conditions These benefits aren't just cosmetic—they're rooted in how hair behaves. When humidity rises, water moves into the hair unevenly, causing the strand to swell and disrupting its shape. That's what creates frizz. By helping regulate moisture movement across the cuticle, silicones can improve smoothness and definition while reducing unwanted expansion. Why Silicone Gets a Bad Reputation Not all silicones behave the same way. Some traditional silicones, like dimethicone, are less water-soluble and can build up over time if they're used repeatedly without an effective cleansing routine. That buildup—not the silicone itself—is what can leave hair feeling heavy, coated, or dull. Many newer silicone technologies work differently. Lightweight silicones, including ingredients like amodimethicone, cyclomethicone, and dimethiconol, are designed to provide conditioning, shine, and heat protection while rinsing away more easily within a typical shampoo routine. The conversation around silicone became especially prominent through curly hair routines like the Curly Girl Method, which often minimize or eliminate silicones, which specifically uses co-washing (no shampoo) as the primary cleansing step. In that routine, non-water-soluble silicones genuinely accumulate, because there's nothing in the wash cycle capable of removing them. The advice to avoid heavy silicones made perfect sense within that context. In those routines, avoiding heavier silicones makes sense because they're not regularly being removed. Over time, that advice expanded beyond its original context, turning "silicone-free" into a universal marketing message. In reality, the best choice depends entirely on your hair type, styling habits, and how often you use a clarifying shampoo. Here’s where things get interesting. Many products labeled “silicone-free” replace silicones with waxes or heavy oils, which can also form barriers and create dulling, hydration-blocking buildup if not properly removed. In other words, a product with a “silicone-free” callout does not automatically guarantee the healthiest results! How Silicone Works for Different Hair Types Hair type influences how hair reacts to moisture, heat, and styling products. Your hair type shapes your daily care routine and styling choices. Porosity, thickness, and texture greatly influence how silicones behave. Straight Hair Straight hair typically has a flatter, tighter cuticle that naturally allows oils to travel easily from scalp to ends. Because of that, heavier silicones can sometimes leave hair feeling weighed down more quickly. Lightweight silicone-containing products, however, can still be incredibly beneficial. Heat protectants and lightweight styling products can help reduce static, add shine, and protect against thermal damage without sacrificing movement. Wavy Hair Wavy hair often sits between straight and curly hair in both structure and moisture needs. It tends to be more susceptible to frizz because the cuticle isn't perfectly uniform along the wave pattern. Lightweight silicones can help smooth the cuticle, support wave definition, and reduce humidity-induced frizz while maintaining softness and bounce. Curly Hair Curly hair naturally loses moisture more easily because the cuticle is more lifted and the curl pattern makes it harder for natural scalp oils to travel down the strand. For curls, silicone can help lock in hydration after moisturizing products have been applied, reduce tangling, improve slip, and create longer-lasting curl definition. The key is choosing formulas that balance moisture with effective cleansing. Coily Hair Coily hair has the greatest need for moisture retention and experiences the highest amount of friction during detangling and protective styling. Silicone can help reduce breakage by improving slip, minimizing friction between strands, and helping seal moisture into the hair. Regular cleansing remains important, but avoiding silicone altogether isn't necessary for many coily hair routines. Should You Avoid Silicone? The better question isn't "Is this silicone-free?" It's: Which silicone is being used? Does this formula match my hair type? Does my wash routine remove buildup when needed? Hair care works best when every product in your routine works together. If you're using heavier styling products, an occasional clarifying shampoo or a double cleanse can help remove buildup. If you're using lightweight conditioning silicones as part of a balanced routine, they may provide exactly the smoothness, shine, and frizz control your hair needs. The Bottom Line Hair care isn't about avoiding ingredients; it's about understanding them. Silicone remains one of the most effective ingredients available for improving shine, reducing friction, protecting against heat, and helping manage frizz. Whether it's the right choice depends on your hair's structure, your styling habits, and your overall routine. At Function of Beauty, we believe the best routine starts with your hair type and not with marketing claims. Because when you understand how your hair works, choosing the right products becomes a whole lot easier.
articles.title: Silicone in Hair Care: Separating the Myths from the Science

articles.summary: Have you ever used a conditioner that someone swears by, only to wonder if you accidentally bought the wrong bottle? Their hair is soft, smooth, and shiny. Yours feels flat, greasy, dry, coated, or somehow looks no different. Chances are, the conditioner is not the problem. The same formula can perform differently because hair care isn't one-size-fits-all. Your hair type, strand thickness, density, condition, damage, and the way you apply products can all influence the result. And to understand why, lets breakdown what conditioner is actually designed to do. The Science of How Conditioner Works Hair naturally carries an electrical charge, and that charge can become more pronounced when the hair surface is weathered or damaged. Heat styling, chemical treatments, friction, and changes to the hair's protective surface can all affect how the fiber behaves. The hair cuticle affects electrical charge based on how flat or damaged its scales are. Healthy cuticles keep a neutral or slightly negative charge, while damaged cuticles create a strong negative charge that causes static and frizz. Conditioners use the law of electrical attraction to fix hair damage by matching positive charges in the product to the negative charges on the hair cuticle. Conditioners contain positively charged ingredients called cationic conditioning agents, which are attracted to negatively charged areas of the hair fiber. These ingredients deposit onto the hair surface to help reduce static and friction, improve slip, and leave hair feeling smoother and easier to manage. But conditioning isn't one-size-fits-all. Different hair structures distribute natural oils differently. Fine hair can become weighed down more easily than thicker hair. Damaged areas may behave differently from healthier sections of the very same strand. A curl pattern changes the way hair bends, tangles, retains its shape, and experiences dryness along its length. That's why two people can use the exact same conditioner and have completely different results. Hair type is one part of the picture. Strand thickness, density, porosity, damage, treatment history, and product application add another layer to what your hair needs. The formula isn't the only thing that matters. How you apply conditioner matters, too. Putting a blob of conditioner on your scalp is not setting you up for clean-looking hair. You also have different types of conditioners that have different application techniques: Rinse-out conditioners, hair masks, and leave-in treatments are designed to do different jobs. Using the right product in the wrong way can make even a great product feel too heavy on your hair. Why Hair Type Matters The difference between straight, wavy, curly, and coily hair comes down primarily to the visible geometry of the hair fiber. That geometry influences how hair behaves, how easily natural scalp oils can travel along the strand, where friction occurs, and how much conditioning support the lengths may need. Hair type is not a complete diagnosis. Two people with curly hair can have completely different strand thicknesses, densities, levels of damage, and conditioning needs. The same is true for every hair type. Think of hair type as the starting point, not the final answer. Straight Hair Straight hair has little to no natural bend along the fiber, creating a relatively direct path from scalp to ends. That can allow natural scalp oils to travel more easily along the hair shaft than they do through highly curved or tightly coiled hair. It can also mean that some straight hair becomes oily or weighed down more quickly, particularly when conditioner is applied heavily near the roots. For fine or low-density straight hair especially, a heavy conditioning routine can leave strands looking flat rather than healthy. The Straight Hair Conditioner, formulated with avocado oil, is designed to condition and smooth without unnecessary heaviness. Apply it primarily from the mid-lengths through the ends, especially if your roots tend to become oily, and rinse thoroughly. For deeper conditioning, swap in the Straight Hair Mask once a week. Its seaweed extract helps support a smooth-looking hair surface and reflective shine. Leave it on for 5 to 10 minutes before rinsing. A lightweight leave-in can also be useful for dry or damaged ends. The key is to use only what your hair needs. Fine straight hair often benefits more from strategic conditioning than from layering multiple heavy products. Wavy Hair Wavy hair can have competing needs along the same length. Roots may become oily or experience buildup, while the bends and curves through the mid-lengths and ends can feel drier, frizzier, or less defined. Add variation in strand thickness and density, and one conditioning strategy won't work for everyone. The solution isn't necessarily a heavier conditioner. The solution might include adding moisturizing products to your routine. The Wavy Hair Conditioner, formulated with argan oil, can be applied from around ear level through the ends, concentrating on the areas that need the most conditioning and keeping the product away from the scalp if your roots tend to become oily. For deeper conditioning, replace your regular conditioner with the Wavy Hair Mask once or twice a week. Its vegan squalane formula provides additional conditioning support without requiring you to overload the hair every wash day. Leave it on for 5 to 10 minutes before rinsing. The Wavy Leave-In Treatment can help support softness and manageability between washes, especially through dry or damaged lengths. The goal is to moisturize and condition the lengths without automatically assuming that every wash requires the same level of conditioning. Curly Hair Curly hair's bends, loops, and spirals can make it more difficult for natural scalp oils to travel evenly from the roots to the ends. As a result, the lengths can be more prone to dryness, tangling, and friction. Curly hair can also experience mechanical stress at the points where the strand bends. Damage, porosity, strand thickness, and styling habits will all influence how much conditioning support an individual routine needs. The Curly Hair Conditioner, formulated with Jamaican black castor oil and hemp seed protein, is designed to provide conditioning and slip while supporting detangling. Apply it generously through the lengths and use your fingers or a wide-tooth comb to gently work through tangles while the conditioner is in the hair. Let it sit for a few minutes before rinsing. For additional conditioning, use the Custom SOS Curly Hair Mask in place of conditioner once or twice a week and leave it on for around 10 minutes. For best results, follow with the Curly Leave-In Treatment on damp hair. This creates an additional conditioning layer that can support softness, manageability, and reduced friction as the hair dries. For styling, apply Super Shape Curl Cream to wet hair to help define your natural curl pattern while maintaining flexibility. For curly hair, conditioning isn't simply about adding more of the same product; it's layering in moisture products and applying a mask regularly. Coily Hair The main thing to keep in mind when caring for coily hair is consistent conditioning. Coily hair's tight bends and curves can make it more difficult for natural oils from the scalp to travel evenly through the lengths, which is why the hair can be more prone to dryness, tangling, and breakage. Start with a Coily Hair Shampoo that cleanses the scalp and hair without leaving the lengths feeling overly stripped. Follow with a Coily Hair Conditioner to help provide slip, softness, and easier detangling. Work the conditioner through the mid-lengths and ends, taking time to gently distribute it through the hair before rinsing. For additional conditioning support, swap your regular conditioner for a Coily Hair Mask once or twice a week. This gives your hair a more intensive conditioning treatment and can help support softness and manageability. Leave the mask on for 5 to 10 minutes before rinsing, then adjust the frequency based on how your hair responds. The goal isn't to use the most products or the richest formula. It's to create a routine that works with your hair's structure and gives your strands the cleansing and conditioning support they need. Do You Wonder How You Use Your Conditioner? Finding the right conditioner is only part of the equation. How you apply it and rinse it can change the result. Your scalp and your lengths don't necessarily have the same needs. Your scalp naturally produces sebum, while the mid-lengths and ends are farther from the source of those natural oils. For many people, concentrating conditioner through the lengths and ends, rather than applying it heavily at the roots, can help provide conditioning where it's needed without leaving the scalp area feeling weighed down. If your roots regularly feel oily or flat after wash day while your ends still feel dry, the formula may not be the only thing to reconsider. You may simply need to adjust where you're applying your conditioner, how much you're using, or how thoroughly you're rinsing. Why Rinsing Your Conditioner Properly Matters Rinsing is where your conditioning routine comes together. Too little rinsing can leave excess product behind, causing hair to feel heavy, coated, or greasy. But rinsing until your hair feels completely stripped isn't the goal either. Start with comfortably lukewarm water and allow it to flow through the lengths of your hair, helping to remove excess product. Avoid excessively hot water, which can leave the hair and scalp feeling dry or uncomfortable. If you enjoy finishing with cooler water, you can, but what matters most is using a comfortable temperature and rinsing thoroughly enough for your hair and the amount of product you've used. As you rinse, gently guide your hair downward with your fingers, following the natural direction of the strands. There's no need to scrub, bunch, or aggressively move the hair around. Instead, let the water do most of the work while you gently separate the lengths and help rinse away excess conditioner. This can be particularly helpful for hair that is prone to tangling, including curly and coily textures. Use the feel of your hair and your hair type as your guide. Continue rinsing until it no longer feels heavily coated but still feels soft and manageable. Straight hair looks and feels cleaner if all of the conditioner is thoroughly rinsed. For curly and coily hair, your goal isn't to remove every trace of conditioning from the hair. The goal isn't to use the richest conditioner or the most products. It's to understand how your hair type behaves, then build a conditioning routine around it. Better hair days start with a Function hair type routine.
articles.title: The Real Reason Conditioner Isn't One-Size-Fits-All
